extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, courts, and practitioners applying the FLSA economic reality test
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance for deciding whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the Fair Labor Standards Act using the economic reality test. Focuses on economic dependence and enumerates factors to be used as guideposts in a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence as the ultimate inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic dependence is the ultimate inquiry for determining whether a worker is an independent contractor or an employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis focuses on whether the worker is in business for themself and whether the worker is economically dependent on the (potential) employer for work. Economic dependence does not focus on the amount the worker earns or whether the worker has other sources of income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test in which factors are guides to be used together rather than being pre-weighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factors are not exhaustive and no single factor is dispositive. The Department returns to the longstanding totality approach rather than an ABC or 'core factors' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the extent of control the potential employer exercises over the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider scheduling, remote supervision, price setting, the ability to work for others, reservable/retained rights, and compliance with legal obligations when assessing control. The final rule provides broader discussion of how these elements should be considered under the control factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the worker's investment in facilities and equipment as a separate factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investment should be framed as a separate factor and considered in terms of whether the investment is integral to the potential employer's business (as opposed to an integrated unit of production). The Department revised regulatory text regarding the investment factor after comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the worker has opportunities for profit or risk of loss from the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the traditional economic reality factors (noted in Silk) used to inform whether a worker is operating a business or is economically dependent on the employer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the permanency or duration of the worker's relationship with the potential employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanency is relevant to economic dependence and the final rule discusses exclusivity in the context of the permanency factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill required / initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree of skill required for the work and the worker's initiative, judgment, and energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule discusses initiative in the context of the skill factor: whether the worker depends on their own initiative, judgment, and energy for success versus being directed as part of the employer's enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral part / integrated unit of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the worker's services are an integral part of the potential employer's business or integrated unit of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department consider whether a worker's tasks are integral to the employer's business—this supports an employee finding if the worker is part of the integrated unit of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: No single factor is controlling or dispositive in the economic reality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each factor should be considered in context; the presence or absence of any one factor alone does not determine status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors are illustrative, not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed economic reality factors are illustrative guideposts; other relevant facts may be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that additional factors can arise in particular factual scenarios and should be incorporated into the totality analysis as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence focuses on dependence for work not income
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic dependence examines whether a worker is dependent on a particular business for continued work, not whether the worker depends on income for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects a 'dependence-for-income' approach. Other sources of income or the amount of pay are generally not relevant to the economic dependence inquiry, though a worker can still be economically dependent even if they work for others or are independently wealthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statutory definitions and 'suffer or permit' breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis must be guided by the FLSA's statutory definitions (employ, employee, employer) and the 'suffer or permit to work' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act's broad definitions and legislative purpose to reach varied working relationships should inform the totality analysis; the test must align with the statutory text and judicial precedent recognizing expansive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology to avoid predetermination ('potential employer')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the phrase 'worker's potential employer' rather than simply 'employer' to avoid implying a predetermined outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopted edits throughout the regulatory text to use 'potential employer' in places where using 'employer' might suggest a result already determined.
